title: Ezekiel 38:1–9
context: Ezekiel 38:1–9 begins the first oracle against Gog, spoken by the LORD to the prophet. Ezekiel is to set his face toward “Gog, of the land of Magog, the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal” (38:2). The word rendered Rosh can also mean chief or head, and many translations read the phrase as chief prince of Meshech and Tubal instead of a people named Rosh. Gog is not otherwise known with certainty; ancient and modern readers have proposed links with a historical ruler, such as a king of Lydia, or have taken Gog as a representative or symbolic figure. Magog, Meshech, Tubal, Gomer, and Togarmah appear among the descendants of Japheth in Genesis 10:2–3, and Cush and Put among the sons of Ham in Genesis 10:6; Meshech, Tubal, and Togarmah also appear as traders in Ezekiel 27:13–14. Persia is to the east, and Cush and Put are commonly taken as peoples of Africa, south and west of Egypt. Many locate these northern peoples in the region of modern Turkey and the lands around the Black Sea; theories that map them onto particular modern nations are debated, and the oracle’s own emphasis is on a coalition from the far north and from the ends of the known world. The LORD says he will turn Gog around and put hooks into his jaws (38:4; compare 29:4) and bring him against a land restored from the sword, whose people dwell securely, “In the latter years” (38:8). How God’s sovereignty relates to the invader’s own designs may be compared with the box at Judges 9:23. Readers take the prophecy in several ways: as an oracle with a near historical horizon, as symbolic or idealist language for the final defeat of evil, as a future end-time battle in premillennial and other futurist schemes, or, in amillennial and postmillennial readings, as a picture of the final assault on God’s people that Revelation 20:8 takes up; each is held within both traditions.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word came to Ezekiel. Arminian readers note that the Gog oracles follow directly after the promises of restoration in chapter 37, and they see the placement as showing that the restored people will still face a great threat that God himself will overcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same placement and read the oracle as showing God’s protection of the people he has restored. They observe that the sequence of restoration followed by attack and deliverance shapes how readers relate these chapters to later prophecy, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: “Son of man, set your face toward Gog, of the land of Magog, the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal, and prophesy against him,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet to set his face toward “Gog, of the land of Magog, the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal”. Arminian readers note that Rosh may be a people or may mean chief, so that many translations read chief prince, and they hold the identifications loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the names loosely and compare Genesis 10:2, where Magog, Tubal, and Meshech appear among Japheth’s sons. They observe that ancient and modern identifications of Gog and his lands are debated, and they do not tie the prophecy to any single map.

verses.text: and say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says, “Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal.” Arminian readers note that the oracle begins with God’s opposition to Gog, and they see the LORD as the one who determines the outcome of the conflict from the start.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same opening and read it as declaring God’s sovereign judgment on the enemy of his people. They observe that the formula I am against you appears elsewhere in Ezekiel’s oracles concerning foreign peoples, and both traditions read it as shared ground.

verses.text: I will turn you around, and put hooks into your jaws, and I will bring you out, with all your army, horses and horsemen, all of them clothed in full armor, a great company with buckler and shield, all of them handling swords;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will turn you around, and put hooks into your jaws, and I will bring you out”. Arminian readers note the echo of 29:4, “I will put hooks in your jaws”, spoken of Pharaoh, and they see Gog as a powerful enemy still under God’s control.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and read the hooks as showing that Gog is led where God intends. They observe that the relation between God’s leading and Gog’s own plans may be compared with the box at Judges 9:23, and they read the verse as shared ground on God’s rule over the nations.

verses.text: Persia, Cush, and Put with them, all of them with shield and helmet;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Persia, Cush, and Put will be with Gog. Arminian readers note that Persia lies to the east and that Cush and Put are commonly taken as peoples of Africa, and they see the list as describing a coalition drawn from the ends of the known world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same breadth and compare Genesis 10:6, where Cush and Put appear among Ham’s sons. They hold the exact identifications loosely, and they read the list as stressing the scale of the threat rather than offering a precise political map.

verses.text: Gomer, and all his hordes; the house of Togarmah in the uttermost parts of the north, and all his hordes—even many peoples with you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD names Gomer and its hordes and the house of Togarmah in the uttermost parts of the north. Arminian readers note that Gomer and Togarmah appear in Genesis 10:2–3, and they see them as northern peoples whose exact locations are debated, often placed in the region of modern Turkey.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the locations loosely and note that Togarmah appears as a trader in Ezekiel 27:14. They observe that modern theories mapping these names onto particular nations are debated, and both traditions decline to make such theories a point of contrast.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Be prepared, yes, prepare yourself, you, and all your companies who are assembled to you, and be a guard to them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Be prepared, yes, prepare yourself, you, and all your companies who are assembled to you”. Arminian readers note the ironic tone, as God invites Gog to prepare for a battle in which he will be defeated, and they see God’s confidence in the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same irony and read the command as showing that Gog’s preparations serve God’s purpose. They observe that the verse may also be read as calling Gog to be a guard for his allies, and they hold the precise sense open.

verses.text: After many days you will be visited. In the latter years you will come into the land that is brought back from the sword, that is gathered out of many peoples, on the mountains of Israel, which have been a continual waste; but it is brought out of the peoples and they will dwell securely, all of them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that “In the latter years” Gog will come against a land brought back from the sword, whose people dwell securely. Arminian readers note that the attack follows Israel’s restoration, and they hold open whether the latter years point to a near or a final horizon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same setting and observe that readers place it in different frames: a historical horizon, a symbolic picture of the final conflict, or a future end-time event. They do not choose between these readings, which are held within both traditions.

verses.text: You will ascend. You will come like a storm. You will be like a cloud to cover the land, you and all your hordes, and many peoples with you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Gog will come like a storm and a cloud to cover the land, with many peoples. Arminian readers note the vivid images of overwhelming force, and they see the threat as one that would seem unstoppable to a people dwelling without defenses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same images and read them as heightening the contrast with God’s deliverance that follows. They observe that the storm and cloud are poetic pictures, and both traditions read the verse as shared ground on the scale of the danger God will overcome.
